extraction.name: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
extraction.description: This paper presents a systematic study of object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs). It evaluates several representative LVLMs on MSCOCO using CHAIR and proposes a polling-based query method called POPE for more stable and flexible evaluation of object hallucination. The study also analyzes how visual instruction data distributions, including frequently appearing and co-occurring objects, influence hallucination.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.citeAs: Li, Yifan; Du, Yifan; Zhou, Kun; Wang, Jinpeng; Zhao, Wayne Xin; Wen, Ji-Rong. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The evaluation data are built from existing image datasets. For CHAIR evaluation, the authors randomly sample 2,000 images from the validation set of MSCOCO with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions. For POPE on MSCOCO, they randomly select 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in the annotations and construct 6 questions per image. POPE constructs triples consisting of an image, multiple object-probing questions, and Yes/No answers. Ground-truth objects are obtained either from human annotations or automatic segmentation results from SEEM, and nonexistent objects are sampled under Random, Popular, and Adversarial settings.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data come from existing datasets including MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA. The study uses images, object annotations, and human-labeled captions from these datasets, and also uses segmentation outputs generated by SEEM for annotation-free POPE construction.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For CHAIR, the authors prompt LVLMs with caption-generation instructions and compute hallucination metrics on generated captions. For POPE, they convert hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by templating questions of the form "Is there a/an <object> in the image?" They set the ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects to 1:1 for label balance and devise three negative sampling strategies: Random Sampling, Popular Sampling, and Adversarial Sampling.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For computing CHAIR on MSCOCO, the paper follows prior settings that only consider 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge. For CHAIR evaluation, 2,000 images are randomly sampled from the MSCOCO validation set. For POPE on MSCOCO, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects are randomly selected, and 6 questions are constructed for each image. For unannotated settings, images are automatically annotated using SEEM segmentation results before POPE question construction.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations for POPE are derived either from existing human annotations in datasets or from automatic segmentation using SEEM. POPE uses ground-truth objects to create positive Yes questions and sampled nonexistent objects to create negative No questions. In SEEM-based POPE, probing objects are selected from the segmentation results of SEEM on the datasets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes stability, scalability, and consistency of the annotation/evaluation process. It reports that POPE is more stable than CHAIR across prompt templates. It also compares SEEM-based POPE with annotation-based POPE and notes performance gaps due to finer granularity and possible inconsistency between SEEM label sets and collected human annotations. The paper further validates consistency by checking whether objects receiving "No" responses appear in generated captions and whether objects mentioned in captions receive "Yes" responses.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 6 questions per image for POPE on MSCOCO
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that hallucination hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment and may result in unexpected consequences caused by hallucinated objects. It gives the example that an autonomous driving system could make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events due to incorrect understanding of the external environment, leading to serious safety issues. The authors hope the work can bring insights for developing more reliable and human-aligned LVLMs.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper empirically reveals that object distributions in visual instruction datasets affect hallucination. LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects in the visual instruction datasets and objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects in the image. It also notes that synthetic visual instructions generated by unimodal LLMs may involve unexpected descriptive information inconsistent with the image, which could mislead LVLMs.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper lists several limitations: it only focuses on object hallucination and does not measure overall LVLM capability; due to computation limits, all models are evaluated on only part of each validation set, so results may be affected by data distribution; POPE uses a matching-based method to determine whether models answer Yes or No, and models may fail to provide explicit Yes/No words, causing inaccurate evaluation; when combined with automatic segmentation, object labels may be inconsistent with human annotations, leading to divergence in results; and only a small number of LVLMs are compared, excluding some recently released or closed-source models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The data are used for evaluation of object hallucination in LVLMs. CHAIR is used to evaluate hallucination in image captioning tasks, and POPE is proposed as a stable, fair, and flexible evaluation approach that can also be extended to unannotated datasets. The paper also uses the constructed evaluation data to compare hallucination with performance on VQA and image captioning tasks.
